questions.prompt: Which view should take extra width, and which should give up width? Explain the separate jobs of hugging and compression resistance.
questions.scenario: The title prefers 180 points, the badge 60, and spacing uses 12. The parent gives the row either 300 or 220 points. Choose horizontal priorities for the desired behavior.
questions.androidBridge: ConstraintLayout and Compose measurement help frame size negotiation, but Swift intrinsic-size priorities are optional inequalities, not Kotlin layout weights or Compose hard constraints. Raising hugging does not raise compression resistance.
rubric: Explains hugging as resistance to growth and compression resistance as resistance to shrinking.
Calculates 48 extra points and a 32-point shortage.
Chooses separate horizontal priorities from the intended behavior.
Explains how a known narrower width can make multiline text taller.
Identifies required-rule conflicts and a fallback when minimum readable widths cannot fit.
questions.answerHTML:
Intrinsic content size is a view's preferred size. Hugging resists growing beyond it; compression resistance resists becoming smaller. The row prefers 180 + 60 + 12 = 252 points. At 300 it has 48 extra points: lower title hugging lets the title grow. At 220 it lacks 32 points: lower title compression resistance makes the title narrow first. These are separate preferences.

A multiline title can convert narrower width into additional height, provided its width is determined and vertical constraints allow growth. The arithmetic predicts negotiation, not real font measurements. Inspect the actual instance priorities rather than assuming every control uses identical defaults. Required priority is 1000. Incompatible rules all marked required cannot be satisfied together. If the badge and minimum readable title cannot fit, change to a vertical arrangement or another declared overflow policy. Verify narrow width, long localized text, and accessibility text sizes before accepting the row.
followUps: What if title width is undetermined or it allows only one line?
How would you verify which view gives way without equal competing priorities?
pitfalls: Expecting high hugging to prevent truncation.
Calling the invented width calculation a device measurement.

questions.prompt: Why is the form's bottom space doubled while the focused field stays hidden? Trace who adds space and choose who handles keyboard avoidance.
questions.scenario: A UIKit controller adds safe-area spacing. A scroll wrapper adjusts content insets, the padding inside its scrolling area. A hosted SwiftUI child also moves content away from the keyboard.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose WindowInsets consumption suggests tracing inset ownership. UIKit safe areas, scroll adjustment, and keyboardLayoutGuide have distinct contracts; they do not follow Compose inset-consumption rules or automatically describe a floating keyboard.
rubric: Traces spacing through controller, scroll wrapper, and hosted child.
Distinguishes safe-area, readable-width, keyboard, and scroll-content guides.
Chooses one keyboard-avoidance owner and keeps fields reachable.
Checks controller containment and this component's sizing contract.
Plans narrow-window, large-text, and floating-keyboard checks.
questions.answerHTML:
List every source of bottom space: controller constraints, automatic scroll adjustment, explicit insets, and the hosted child's behavior. An inset is added spacing. A safe area avoids obscuring system or container UI, but does not fully describe keyboard overlap. Readable-width and margin guides serve separate horizontal purposes. Removing all safe areas may hide the gap while putting controls under system UI.

Choose one keyboard-avoidance owner. UIKit's keyboardLayoutGuide can express keyboard relationships, while a scrolling form may instead manage keyboard-aware insets and scroll the active field into view. Floating keyboards require a deliberate policy. Constrain scroll content to its content guide and viewport width appropriately so large text can grow vertically. Check child-controller containment, hosting sizing, and the specific component's safe-area contract together; a local bridge convention is not universal guidance. Verify focus, dismissal, resizing, and accessibility text in a running scratch target. A corrected inset calculation alone does not prove the field is reachable or editing state survives.
followUps: How would you distinguish repeated insets from incorrect scroll-content height?
What must you verify with an undocked iPad keyboard?
pitfalls: Ignoring every safe area to remove the gap.
Expecting keyboard avoidance to supply focus or a number-pad Done action.

questions.prompt: Why can a diffable list have the right item IDs but show old text? Explain how to update content and configure the existing cell completely.
questions.scenario: The snapshot lists [A, B]. A's subtitle changes in the content lookup, but its ID stays A. Later C is inserted and the order becomes [C, B, A].
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java RecyclerView stable IDs and DiffUtil suggest separating item identity from displayed content. UIKit snapshots use Hashable identifiers and explicit reconfiguration; RecyclerView payload and onBindViewHolder behavior is not an exact counterpart.
rubric: Separates item ID, current position, cell object, and cell reuse identifier.
Keeps changing subtitle content out of stable identity.
Updates the lookup and explicitly reconfigures surviving changed IDs.
Explains that reconfiguration does not call prepareForReuse.
Resolves selection by current item ID after insertion or reorder.
questions.answerHTML:
A diffable snapshot lists stable item IDs and their order. Changing A's subtitle elsewhere does not necessarily configure A's cell again. Update the content lookup, then explicitly mark changed IDs that remain in the snapshot for reconfiguration. Keep A's identity unchanged. New C gets initial configuration rather than reconfiguration. Each ID must be unique across the snapshot.

Do not synthesize identity from the entire mutable display model: changing a subtitle could then look like replacing the item. Reconfiguration preserves an existing cell and does not call prepareForReuse for that update, so configuration must set every relevant visual and accessibility property. Reserve reload behavior for changes such as needing a different cell kind. Apply content and snapshot through one serialized UI owner so their updates cannot interleave incorrectly. Selection should resolve or capture A's domain ID rather than offset zero, which becomes C after insertion. Test subtitle changes, reorder, duplicate IDs, and delayed image completion separately.
followUps: When should you reload rather than reconfigure a cell?
How would you keep a late old image from appearing in a reused cell?
pitfalls: Hashing changing display fields as permanent identity.
Expecting prepareForReuse to clear every reconfiguration.

questions.prompt: How would you prevent duplicate page loads and old query errors? Explain why canceling thumbnail prefetch must respect visible consumers.
questions.scenario: Repeated end-of-list events start cursor p1 twice. Query B succeeds, then query A fails and replaces B's results. Canceling prefetch also cancels an image still needed by a visible row.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine jobs and RecyclerView prefetch offer ownership analogies. Swift actor isolation does not make response order equal page order, and UIKit prefetch cancellation expresses predicted interest rather than ownership of every shared request.
rubric: Guards each active cursor within its query generation.
Rejects old successes and old failures.
Clears only the matching request's active marker.
Loads visible content even if prefetch never happens.
Separates one consumer losing interest from cancellation of a shared resource.
questions.answerHTML:
A cursor identifies the next page; a query generation identifies the current search. The page owner keeps both, the active cursor, ordered IDs, and whether paging ended. Start only if that generation and cursor have no active request. Capture them before waiting and check them on success and failure before changing rows, errors, or active markers. An old completion must not unlock newer work. Serialize loads or explicitly buffer out-of-order pages.

Preserve useful rows on a later-page failure and retry the failed cursor under the same guard. Define duplicate-ID merging and repeated-cursor behavior. Prefetch is a separate resource-interest mechanism: translate callback positions to current IDs, and ensure visible configuration can load missing content without any prefetch callback. Canceling one speculative interest should not cancel a shared image still needed by a visible consumer. Use controlled start signals and completion gates to release B before A, then exercise A's success and error paths.
followUps: What should an empty page with another cursor mean?
Which assertions separately prove no duplicate loads and no old-result updates?
pitfalls: Checking query generation only for success.
Making prefetch the only way required content loads.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI ask a child for size and then place it? Define the column's behavior for unspecified, zero, finite, and unbounded width proposals.
questions.scenario: A custom column measures multiline Text in a narrow parent and a vertical ScrollView. It currently turns every nil proposed dimension into zero.
questions.androidBridge: Compose measure and placement provide a useful sequence, but ProposedViewSize is a proposal rather than Compose Constraints. A nil Swift dimension asks for ideal behavior; it is not Kotlin null meaning an absent child.
rubric: Separates the proposed size, reported size, and placement.
Distinguishes unspecified, zero, and unbounded probes.
Explains why narrower multiline text can grow taller.
Uses consistent measurement and placement, including the bounds origin.
Keeps networking and observable-state changes out of sizing methods.
questions.answerHTML:
A proposal asks how much room a child would use. The child reports a size; the parent then places it. SwiftUI may ask several times. An unspecified dimension asks for ideal behavior, zero asks about minimum behavior, and infinity probes maximum behavior. Turning nil into zero changes the question and can collapse text. The reported concrete size still needs a meaningful finite answer.

For a finite column width, measure text with that width and sum the returned heights plus spacing between children. Place using a consistent width policy and the final bounds origin. A narrower multiline Text may become taller, so cached measurements must remain valid for the actual inputs. Empty children should not create a phantom gap. A vertical ScrollView commonly leaves the scrolling dimension unspecified rather than imposing viewport height. Define overflow behavior for children that exceed the budget. Layout methods can run repeatedly, so they are unsuitable lifecycle hooks for networking or state mutation. Verify different probes and final rendering separately.
followUps: How could a main-child GeometryReader change the size being measured?
Which changed inputs would invalidate cached multiline measurements?
pitfalls: Treating a proposal as a mandatory exact size.
Reporting infinity as the layout's concrete height.

questions.prompt: Why does the scroll control flicker with two geometry reporters? Define how contributions combine, compare positions in one coordinate space, and trace layout feedback.
questions.scenario: A bottom-marker PreferenceKey originally overwrote its contributions. A second child now reports geometry. Showing the scroll control itself changes the measured content.
questions.androidBridge: Compose onGloballyPositioned offers a geometry-observation analogy, but SwiftUI PreferenceKey reduces descendant contributions upward. Kotlin callback order and Compose coordinates do not define SwiftUI reduction or layout-feedback semantics.
rubric: Identifies the original assumption of one reporting child.
Chooses a meaningful combining rule for several reports.
Compares positions in the same named coordinate space.
Traces geometry changing state, state changing layout, and layout changing geometry.
Avoids unchanged-value updates and keeps the control from destabilizing its threshold.
questions.answerHTML:
Preference reduction means combining child reports into one value for an ancestor. Overwriting worked only under the original single-marker rule. With two reports, the last is not automatically the bottommost. Decide what the ancestor needs: one dedicated marker, a meaningful maximum, or values keyed by ID with an explicit merge. Choose that meaning first rather than whichever reducer happens to stop flicker.

Measure in one named scroll coordinate space with a common origin and axes. A global position and local viewport height are not comparable just because both are numbers. Put an observing GeometryReader in a background or overlay when it should inspect existing assigned geometry rather than become the main sizing child. Then trace the loop: a preference updates state, state shows a control, the control changes geometry, and a new preference reverses the decision. Ignore unchanged values and keep the control's geometry from destabilizing its own threshold. Test keyboard, safe-area, content, and window changes. Prefer direct layout calculation when the value serves only layout rather than interaction.
followUps: When does maximum preserve the needed meaning, and when does it lose identity?
What check distinguishes mismatched coordinates from a feedback loop?
pitfalls: Keeping overwrite reduction without reviewing multiple reports.
Copying every child frame into observable model state.

questions.prompt: What changes immediately in withAnimation, and what changes visually over time? Distinguish transitions, repeated taps, and reduced-motion behavior.
questions.scenario: Expanding a disclosure inserts details. A broad animation modifier also animates errors. Selection is not committed until code waits for the animation's nominal duration.
questions.androidBridge: Compose animate-as-state suggests interpolation toward state, but SwiftUI transactions and insertion transitions have their own scope. Neither a Kotlin delay nor an animation duration is a correctness boundary for delivering a result.
rubric: Makes semantic state correct before visual completion.
Distinguishes changing existing visuals from inserting or removing a child.
Explains animation scope and unrelated simultaneous changes.
Keeps the final meaning correct when animation is interrupted.
Changes motion policy without disabling the action under reduced motion.
questions.answerHTML:
withAnimation attaches animation information to a synchronous state change. The Boolean changes now; eligible visuals move toward the new state over time. It does not delay the business decision or keep async work alive. A transition describes insertion or removal of a child. An opacity transition alone cannot create insertion when the child remains present. Keep the latest expanded value authoritative.

Keep disclosure visibility derived from the latest Boolean, so repeated taps can interrupt interpolation without leaving a contradictory final hierarchy. A value-watching animation modifier can affect other simultaneous changes inside its scope. Narrow that scope if an unrelated error or keyboard adjustment should update directly. Selection delivery needs its own ownership and exactly-once policy; waiting for a nominal duration cannot establish completion or freshness. Reduced motion should change or remove the visual interpolation while preserving the action and final state. Verify rapid toggling, interrupted navigation, and reduced-motion completion in a running target. A static screenshot demonstrates appearance at one instant, not interruption behavior.
followUps: What state might be lost by replacing identity to trigger an effect?
How would you test selection completion without relying on animation duration?
pitfalls: Waiting for animation duration to synchronize result delivery.
Expecting a transition to animate any permanently present property.

questions.prompt: Why does dragging jump, interfere with scrolling, and lose focus after reorder? Fix temporary movement, stable IDs, current scroll context, and field focus.
questions.scenario: Each onChanged adds the full drag translation to a saved offset. Scroll callbacks keep an old proxy. Two text fields use the same focus case.
questions.androidBridge: Compose pointer input and focus requesters suggest transient interaction owners. SwiftUI GestureState reset, gesture precedence, ScrollViewReader proxy scope, and FocusState cases are distinct contracts rather than exact Kotlin API equivalents.
rubric: Renders saved offset plus current translation without repeated accumulation.
Commits once and defines cancellation and movement bounds.
Checks recognizer competition and offers a semantic alternative.
Uses stable current scroll IDs and the current reader proxy.
Gives each field a unique focus case without rebuilding the draft.
questions.answerHTML:
Drag translation is the distance from this gesture's start. Repeatedly adding that whole distance counts earlier movement again. Keep the saved offset separately from temporary GestureState translation and render their sum. Clamp the candidate to allowed bounds if needed, then commit once on successful ending. GestureState resets on cancellation, so canceled temporary movement must not become another committed offset.

A row drag competes with scrolling and navigation recognizers. Define the target region, direction, and minimum distance before choosing simultaneous or higher-priority composition. Those modifiers cannot certify correct arbitration. Provide buttons or accessibility actions for essential operations. After reorder, scroll to a stable domain ID through the proxy inside the current ScrollViewReader context rather than a retained appearance-time closure. Give each field a distinct optional focus case and clear focus explicitly on dismissal. Resizing or keyboard dismissal should preserve the draft owner. Verify cancellation, actual scrolling, focus progression, and alternative input; directly invoking callbacks tests logic but not recognizers.
followUps: Which geometry should limit movement after scene resize?
What evidence shows reorder preserves the intended scroll target and field identity?
pitfalls: Repeatedly accumulating translation measured from gesture start.
Treating highPriorityGesture as a universal scrolling fix.

questions.prompt: Write the text replacement step using UIKit's supplied range. Explain why its units replace the emoji correctly and what remains to check during composition.
questions.scenario: Current text is A🙂B. UIKit supplies NSRange(location: 1, length: 2) and replacement X. Paste and deletion must use this same replacement path.
questions.androidBridge: Java and Kotlin String indexing also exposes UTF-16 units. Swift String.Index is not an integer offset, and its Character iteration follows grapheme clusters; neither Java char arithmetic nor String.count can replace range conversion.
rubric: Converts NSRange against the exact current buffer.
Handles failed conversion without force-unwrapping.
Replaces the entire range with the entire replacement.
Predicts AXB and distinguishes UTF-16 units from Character count.
Protects marked text and identifies separate grapheme-boundary checks.
questions.answerHTML:
Convert UIKit's range against the exact current string before editing it. NSRange here counts UTF-16 units; Swift text indices are not integer character offsets. In A🙂B, the emoji occupies two UTF-16 units, so the supplied range selects it. Replace that whole range with the whole supplied replacement. If conversion fails, return an explicit failure rather than force-unwrapping. The helper's safe replacement step is:

guard let edit = Range(range, in: current) else {
    return nil
}
return current.replacingCharacters(in: edit, with: replacement)

The helper returns an optional String so an invalid range has an explicit failure path. UIKit's range is in UTF-16 units. In A🙂B, the emoji occupies two such units, so location 1 and length 2 replace it with X and produce AXB. The replacement may contain several characters or be empty for deletion; do not process only its first character.

Swift Character count, UTF-8 byte count, and UTF-16 length are different units. Conversion does not prove a fabricated range covers whole grapheme clusters, the user-perceived characters. Check that separately when required. While markedTextRange exists, aggressive rewriting or truncation can break input-method composition and selection. Prefer a raw editing buffer and a declared commit-time validation policy. Test actual paste, selected replacement, caret behavior, and composition in UIKit; the string helper proves only the transformation boundary.
followUps: What happens with an empty replacement or several user-perceived characters?
Why can't a string-helper test establish marked-text or caret behavior?
pitfalls: Treating NSRange.location as a Swift Character offset.
Assuming every range inside a surrogate pair or grapheme must fail conversion.

questions.prompt: Why does the code lose its leading zero, break unfinished composition, and display an old error? Separate editable text, keyboard hints, and submission validation.
questions.scenario: The demo accepts five ASCII digits. It converts text to Int on each keystroke. The number pad has no Return key. Old server validation finishes after the text changes.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin raw text state, InputType, and coroutine revision checks are useful analogies. UIKit keyboardType does not validate input, submitLabel cannot add a missing number-pad Return key, and Swift string units require an explicit rule.
rubric: Keeps the raw String and leading zero.
Defines ASCII-only submission while allowing unfinished editing.
Separates keyboard hints from paste handling and validation.
Rejects old validation successes and failures by input revision.
Provides explicit keyboard dismissal and field-specific repairable errors.
questions.answerHTML:
Keep the code as raw String text. Converting 01234 to Int loses the zero and treats an identifier as a quantity. Submission accepts exactly five ASCII digits, meaning 0 through 9; that is narrower than all Unicode decimal digits. Allow unfinished editing and input-method composition. Decide when to validate instead of rewriting every intermediate buffer, and normalize only what the business rule permits.

The number-pad keyboard assists entry but cannot prevent paste or prove validity. submitLabel changes an available action label; it does not create a Return key on a number pad. Supply an explicit Done action and a hardware-keyboard submit path, clearing focus without clearing buffers. Tag async validation with the input revision and check it before publishing either success or failure. Preserve the draft on server rejection and explain the field needing repair. Localize persistent labels and error text, allowing expansion at large text sizes. Pure rule tests cover leading zeros and invalid characters; actual keyboard, marked-text, selection, and scrolling interactions require separate runtime observations.
followUps: What tests change if non-ASCII decimal digits are allowed?
When should an error appear, and where should invalid submission move focus?
pitfalls: Using keyboard type as the only validator.
Checking freshness only for success and showing an old error.

questions.prompt: Who should own account services, navigation, focus, and drafts in two windows? Explain what resize and scene disconnection should preserve or release.
questions.scenario: Window A edits alpha while B browses beta. A singleton stores selection and presenter for both. Developers assume rotation creates a new screen.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Activity and Android task lifetimes help discuss independent surfaces, but an iOS scene is not one Activity. Resizing does not imply Android configuration recreation, and a scene identifier is not a domain draft ID.
rubric: Separates process, scene, window, controller, and draft lifetimes.
Keeps navigation, presentation, and focus in the initiating scene.
Declares shared versus independent draft editing.
Distinguishes disconnection from permanent session or process destruction.
Invalidates affected scenes and late account work on logout.
questions.answerHTML:
Separate the lifetimes. The process owns shared account services; each scene, an independently managed UI instance, owns its navigation, presentation, selection, and focus. A window displays its hierarchy, and a controller manages a screen or container. The draft follows its editing and storage contract and may outlive that screen. If windows edit one document, choose shared live state, tentative buffers, or conflict resolution explicitly.

Route presentation through the scene or controller receiving the action. Selecting an arbitrary connected scene or global key window can present login in the wrong surface. Resizing changes available geometry; it does not inherently recreate an Android-style configuration instance or justify replacing the model. Scene disconnection can release scene-owned subscriptions and tasks without deleting a durable draft, and the session may reconnect later. Conversely, in-memory state cannot survive process death by itself. Logout must invalidate account-bound presentation, restoration, caches, and old async results in every relevant scene. A declared iPad destination is not evidence that these two-window semantics work.
followUps: How would separate tentative buffers reconcile commits to one draft?
Which state should survive scene disconnection but end on account change?
pitfalls: Using the first connected scene for every presentation.
Assuming resize recreates the controller and draft.

questions.prompt: Plan scene-restoration adoption for this draft feature. Assign owners, compare lightweight scene state with durable drafts, and define tests, rollout, and recovery.
questions.scenario: The feature restores a selected ID globally. After launch, a deleted record, changed account, or second window can reopen an invalid destination.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin SavedStateHandle values and Room-backed drafts suggest separating presentation restoration from data persistence. SceneStorage and AppStorage have different scene versus defaults scopes; neither reproduces Android process-restoration semantics or grants access to a restored record.
rubric: Names scene-restoration, durable-storage, and account-invalidation owners.
Compares lightweight scene state with repository-backed drafts.
Uses a versioned non-sensitive envelope and checks current records.
Requires two-window and process-restart evidence, including failures.
Stages adoption and falls back safely without repeating side effects.
questions.answerHTML:
Restore the place in the interface separately from the user's durable work. Let the scene owner save a small envelope, a versioned record of non-sensitive restoration fields: account marker, draft ID, and optional selection. The repository owns durable drafts; the account owner invalidates old envelopes and late work. Compare SceneStorage for per-scene selection with repository storage for drafts. Shared AppStorage keys may couple windows.

Restore dependencies normally, validate the envelope version and current account, load the draft, and resolve the selection against current data. Unknown versions, corrupt state, deleted records, or account mismatch fall back to a valid root. Do not restore credentials, stale proxies, or automatic submission. Require independent-window, resize, logout-during-load, and process-restart fixtures, measuring successful restoration and safe fallback by cause. Stage adoption for one bounded feature after its actual scene configuration is verified. Keep a recovery path that ignores incompatible envelopes and opens the list while preserving durable drafts. Disabling restoration should not delete user data or imply a completed app-wide scene migration.
followUps: How would you distinguish an invalid envelope from failure to load the durable draft?
What checks must pass before a restored destination becomes visible?
pitfalls: Treating decoded routes as authorization or permission to submit again.
Deleting durable drafts when disabling presentation restoration.

questions.prompt: Choose shared-state and sizing boundaries for the editor, picker, and UIKit summary. How do Cancel and reorder preserve the committed choice?
questions.scenario: The scratch draft holds name, code, and provider A. Review copies them into new local state. The picker changes committed selection when a row is only highlighted.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose state hoisting and AndroidView updates suggest a shared editing owner and an adapter. SwiftUI State preserves a locally owned observable instance, and UIViewRepresentable has distinct creation, update, and proposal-based sizing contracts.
rubric: Keeps raw buffers and committed selection in one scene-owned draft.
Keeps tentative highlight local when Apply is required.
Resolves reordered providers by stable ID.
Updates the UIKit summary from current shared input.
Explains finite-width fitting and distinguishes view insertion from controller containment.
questions.answerHTML:
The scene root owns navigation and one draft. That draft stores raw name and code, the committed provider ID, and current provider content. Review reads the same model instead of copying its initial values into local State that can drift. For an observable model created locally, root State preserves the reference. Editing children get bindings to that owner's fields rather than separate draft stores.

A picker that commits immediately should mutate only on deliberate selection. An Apply-style picker instead owns a tentative highlight and copies it on confirmation; Cancel leaves the prior committed ID untouched. Resolve IDs against current content after insertion or reorder, and block Review if the selected provider disappears. The UIKit representable creates a label once, updates its text from current input, and fits multiline content against finite proposed width. Larger text or narrower width may increase height; unspecified sizing can defer to the bridge's default strategy. A UILabel needs no child-controller containment, whereas a hosted controller does. Verify reorder, cancellation, wrapping, focus dismissal, and shared model identity as separate contracts.
followUps: What should Review do if the selected provider disappears?
What evidence shows the label actually wraps, beyond sizeThatFits compiling?
pitfalls: Creating separate Review state from initial draft values.
Committing tentative picker changes before Cancel.

questions.prompt: Plan acceptance and adoption of the integrated flow. Map risks to owners and evidence, then define rollout gates and recoverable outcomes for old work or invalid selection.
questions.scenario: The demo looked right once. Paging, input-method composition, large text, restoration, and two-window behavior remain unverified.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java unit tests, Android screenshots, and instrumentation tests motivate layered evidence. A Swift logic fake cannot certify UIKit recognizer or IME behavior, and an iOS simulator snapshot does not establish independent-window or physical-device performance.
rubric: Maps sizing, editing, identity, and scene risks to owners.
Chooses focused logic, rendering, and interaction evidence.
Uses explicit event gates for old success and old failure.
Defines bounded adoption and correctness gates.
Keeps selection and restoration recoverable while stating coverage limits.
questions.answerHTML:
Give each risk an owner: the draft owns validation and committed choice, the page owner rejects old queries, the bridge owns sizing updates, and the scene owns navigation and restoration. Compare pure rule tests, images for long text, and running interactions for keyboard and window behavior. One broad end-to-end script may exercise more, but focused checks identify which contract failed.

Use explicit fake start signals, complete B before A, then release both old success and old failure. Assert current rows, error state, selection, and matching in-flight markers. Add reorder-safe selection and Cancel fixtures. Measure the UIKit summary at declared widths and text categories, and observe composition and focused-field reachability in a running target. Stage adoption behind a bounded feature boundary only after applicable gates pass; record unexecuted device or two-window rows as pending. If a selection vanishes or restoration fails, preserve editable buffers and offer a valid root or renewed choice. Retain a known-good flow for recovery, without erasing drafts or treating the teaching reference as completed production work.
followUps: What small fixture catches an old completion clearing a newer active marker?
When should a rendering difference block adoption versus receive a reviewed baseline update?
pitfalls: Claiming one image proves editing, restoration, and task ownership.
Recording new baselines to hide an unexplained regression.

questions.prompt: Define when search timing starts and when correct results become usable. How should signposts cover the whole operation and the smaller mapping step?
questions.scenario: Search waits for data, maps rows, then displays results. The current timer stops immediately after constructing a Task, before that work finishes.
questions.androidBridge: Android trace sections and coroutine timing suggest operation boundaries. Swift signpost interval identity and lifetime still need explicit pairing; constructing a Task, like launching a Kotlin coroutine, does not measure its awaited work.
rubric: Defines start, usable end, fixture, and which attempts count.
Keeps mapping as a nested diagnostic interval.
Uses distinct identities for overlapping intervals and ends success, failure, and cancellation paths.
Separates elapsed time, CPU work, and visible responsiveness.
Records conditions and bounded non-sensitive metadata.
questions.answerHTML:
Start at an accepted search action and stop when correct results are displayed and the agreed interaction works. Record the fixture, cache, device, OS, build, and failure rules. Stopping after Task creation measures scheduling, not the search outcome. Await the work. A signpost interval is a named start and end in a trace; pair it through success, failure, and cancellation.

Keep a separate mapping interval inside the larger operation to test a CPU-transformation hypothesis. Give overlapping operations distinct interval identities while retaining bounded names. Elapsed time includes waiting; Time Profiler can investigate CPU stacks; rendering evidence establishes presentation and responsiveness. These answer different questions. Keep raw observations and failed or canceled outcomes under the declared rule for which attempts count. Metadata should identify bounded phases and fixtures without logging raw queries or account data. A source signpost establishes instrumentation intent only; actual traces and minimally instrumented confirmation runs are still required for a performance claim.
followUps: How would cancellations count in latency and wasted-work reports?
Which evidence separates queue waiting from synchronous mapping CPU?
pitfalls: Timing Task creation as completed search latency.
Claiming a mapping benchmark proves the screen becomes usable sooner.

questions.prompt: What do these samples support? Review averaging device p95 values, adding phase p95 values, calling nearest-rank p50 the median, and deleting failed runs.
questions.scenario: One device group has five samples and another twenty. The report uses nearest-rank percentiles, calls p50 the conventional median, and removes failures.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin benchmark libraries may expose percentile summaries, but a library result does not define the experiment's denominator. Swift array indexing and nearest-rank arithmetic differ only syntactically; cohort and statistical limits remain essential.
rubric: Uses ceil(p times n) minus one for nearest-rank indexing.
Explains why five-sample p95 is the maximum.
Distinguishes nearest-rank p50 from the conventional even-sample median.
Rejects averaging group p95 values or adding unrelated phase p95 values.
Keeps raw order, outcomes, conditions, and sample-count limits.
questions.answerHTML:
A percentile selects a position in ordered observations. Nearest-rank p95 chooses one-based rank ceil(0.95 × n), then subtracts one for an array index. Values 1 through 20 give 19; five samples give the maximum. These are exact sample calculations, not a reliable population tail. Nearest-rank p50 selects the tenth of twenty values. The conventional even-sample median averages the tenth and eleventh.

Keep device cohorts separate. Averaging their p95 values does not produce a fleet percentile; combining raw observations requires an explicit weighting and sampling model. Likewise, total-operation p95 is not generally the sum of phase p95 values, because different operations can be slow in different phases. Retain paired phase observations to attribute the actual tail. Restore failed, canceled, and invalid-preparation records with declared classifications. Report raw samples, count, range, units, estimator, and thermal/cache conditions. More decimal places do not repair a small, drifting, or selectively filtered experiment.
followUps: How would paired phases from each operation explain the slowest searches?
What predeclared preparation rule could justify rerunning a sample?
pitfalls: Calling averaged p95 values a fleet percentile.
Removing slow failures after seeing the numbers.

questions.prompt: What must finish before launch becomes usable? Separate delegate completion, first frame, and first useful interaction, and draw their required dependencies.
questions.scenario: The app assigns its root quickly. Account reconciliation and store migration continue behind a spinner before a deep link can open.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android startup initializers suggest a dependency graph, but iOS process preparation, delegate or scene callbacks, and presentation metrics have different contracts. Completing a callback is not equivalent to Android fully drawn or usable content.
rubric: Includes runtime preparation before app callbacks.
Maps routing dependencies on account and migration readiness.
Defines first frame separately from usable content.
Finds the longest required chain instead of summing concurrent work.
States preparation for terminated-process launch and surviving-process resume.
questions.answerHTML:
Launch includes loading code, runtime setup, and initializers before familiar app callbacks. Creating the root, laying it out, and presenting a frame come later. That first frame may show only a spinner. Define usability separately: required setup has finished, the allowed route is visible, and the first meaningful action works. Neither root assignment nor viewDidAppear alone proves all three.

Draw dependencies explicitly. A consumer needing migrated data waits for migration; an authenticated route waits for account reconciliation. The critical path is the longest required chain of dependent work. Adding concurrent phase durations does not measure it. Extra parallel work can add contention without shortening it. Specify preparation for terminated-process launches, returning-account launches, deep links, and process-surviving resume; do not call every case cold. Record uncertain OS cache state. Use supported launch measurements for first-frame evidence and a defined readiness boundary for usability, then verify the first tap. Source tracing identifies candidate phases, but supplies no timing or completed launch measurement.
followUps: Where should telemetry start if it must observe launch?
How could a faster first frame make the first tap slower?
pitfalls: Ending launch timing at root assignment.
Adding concurrent startup durations as if all were one sequential chain.

questions.prompt: Own a small startup optimization proposal. Compare deferral with dependency or resource reduction, preserve readiness, and set measurement, rollout, and recovery gates.
questions.scenario: The team wants lazy SDK initialization and different framework linkage to improve launch and reduce size. It has no matched baseline.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin lazy initialization and Android APK size analysis suggest tradeoffs. Swift Task creation can inherit MainActor isolation, and static or dynamic iOS linkage has different packaging costs; no fixed per-framework saving follows from the analogy.
rubric: Names dependency-order, feature-readiness, and release-artifact owners.
Compares options against a measured limiting phase.
Preserves account, migration, and instrumentation ordering.
Separates launch, first-interaction, download-size, and installed-size evidence.
Stages one change with behavior recovery or a corrective build.
questions.answerHTML:
First collect comparable launch and exported-artifact baselines, then choose one measured bottleneck. The startup owner protects dependency order; feature owners protect readiness and first-use behavior; the release owner checks packaging. Compare delaying independent initialization with removing unused work or reducing dependencies and resources. Changing static or dynamic linkage needs its own loading and packaging investigation. Framework count alone does not predict a fixed saving.

Classify work as required before presentation, required before usability, or opportunistic. Preserve account reconciliation, migration, and early instrumentation dependencies. Give deferred work a lifetime and failure policy; Task creation inside MainActor code does not automatically move synchronous initialization off the UI executor. Measure first frame, usable route, and first interaction under identical fixtures. Track executable, resources, download, and installed size as separate quantities. Stage one bounded candidate only after correctness and artifact checks. Define recovery as restoring prior initialization order or producing a verified corrective build for packaging changes. Record pending device observations rather than promising gains from the design.
followUps: What evidence shows lazy work merely moved the stall to the first tap?
Which recovery inputs are needed when a binary dependency changes?
pitfalls: Expecting Task to move synchronous startup work off the UI actor.
Using one byte count for both download and installed size.

questions.prompt: How do commit hitches, render hitches, and hangs differ? Choose evidence for each cause of missed scrolling deadlines.
questions.scenario: One trace candidate shows row mapping on the main thread near a missed commit. Another shows expensive compositing after the app commits on time.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android View traversal and RenderThread offer a pipeline analogy. UIKit or SwiftUI commits through Core Animation and downstream rendering have distinct tracks; Android frame-stage names and budgets are not exact iOS counterparts.
rubric: Separates app commit from later rendering and presentation.
Distinguishes motion hitches from discrete unresponsiveness.
Matches missed deadlines with relevant stacks and rendering tracks.
Treats the refresh interval as shared pipeline time.
Confirms with the same gesture and lighter instrumentation.
questions.answerHTML:
A frame passes through UI updates, a Core Animation commit, rendering, and display. Commit means submitting the app's changes. A commit hitch misses that app deadline. A render hitch misses a later rendering deadline despite a timely commit. A hitch disrupts continuous motion; a hang is a period of unresponsiveness, often during a discrete action. The same blocking work can contribute differently depending on when it runs.

For the mapping hypothesis, select a missed commit interval and inspect relevant main-thread stacks and signposts. For the compositing hypothesis, inspect the render portion after the timely commit rather than assuming more background CPU work will help. Refresh cadence supplies deadline context, not a complete allowance for each method. Average CPU can hide a short badly timed burst. Keep gesture, content, image-cache state, text size, and device conditions fixed. After diagnosis, confirm the candidate with lighter instrumentation and the same interaction. A smooth-looking simulator pass or a print count cannot establish physical-device frame behavior.
followUps: How can a background worker contribute to a missed UI deadline?
What would you inspect if commit improves but scrolling still hitches?
pitfalls: Explaining every scrolling issue from average CPU.
Giving each function the entire refresh interval as its budget.

questions.prompt: Why do progress updates repeat sorting, and why does insertion lose row state? Explain what body evaluation counts and what it cannot prove.
questions.scenario: A 500-row list reads progress in its parent, sorts in body, and uses offsets as row IDs. A print statement is treated as a redraw counter.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose recomposition dependencies and stable keys suggest narrowing reads and preserving identity. SwiftUI Observation tracks accessed properties differently from ObservableObject publication, and body evaluation is not a direct Compose recomposition or displayed-frame count.
rubric: Moves unchanged projection to the accepted data-revision boundary.
Narrows progress reads to the relevant leaf.
Uses stable item IDs instead of positions.
Separates evaluation, reconciliation, layout, commit, and display.
Checks correct behavior before claiming fewer measured hitches.
questions.answerHTML:
Reading progress makes the parent depend on it. Each update can reevaluate body and sort rows again, even when the row data is unchanged. Calculate that projection when a new data revision is accepted. Let a relevant leaf read progress, then check whether helper calls or shared aggregate inputs still broaden dependencies. Splitting functions alone does not narrow them. Observation tracks property reads; ObservableObject publication can affect more consumers.

Use stable domain IDs in ForEach. Offsets change after insertion and can attach local state or actions to the wrong row. Preserve the observable owner's lifetime rather than recreating it during body evaluation. A body print counts evaluations with added overhead; it does not count displayed frames. Evaluation, reconciliation, layout, layer commit, and presentation are separate work. Prove sorting semantics, insertion identity, titles, actions, and cancellation before timing. Correlate update duration with actual hitch intervals and confirm on a matched gesture. Do not claim the dependency cleanup eliminates image decode or render-server cost.
followUps: How can passing one changing aggregate to every row keep updates broad?
What fixture catches an equality shortcut that hides a changed action?
pitfalls: Counting body prints as displayed frames.
Using offsets as stable identity after insertion.

questions.prompt: What stays independent when you copy a Swift Array, and what storage can remain shared? Explain old versions, short slices, and class elements.
questions.scenario: History retains old arrays while editing the newest. Another component keeps a short ArraySlice after the original array binding is released.
questions.androidBridge: Assigning a Kotlin List usually shares a reference; the read-only interface does not promise an independent snapshot. Swift Array preserves value semantics with possible shared storage, but arrays of class instances still share the referenced objects.
rubric: Separates observable value independence from immediate storage copying.
Explains shared versus uniquely owned mutation.
Identifies retained old buffers and slice backing storage.
Distinguishes copying element references from copying class objects.
Separates semantic checks, allocation evidence, and synchronization.
questions.answerHTML:
Two assigned arrays behave as separate values, even if they initially share storage. Copy-on-write separates shared storage when mutation needs it; a uniquely owned mutation may avoid that copy. Check that the original value stays unchanged without promising a particular allocation instruction. Compiler optimization and bridging affect those details. Keeping old versions while changing the newest can keep multiple buffers alive.

An ArraySlice can retain a large backing allocation even when its visible range is small. Converting the needed range to a small Array trades immediate copying for potentially releasing that backing storage. Measure the actual allocation and retention under an equivalent optimized configuration. If elements are class instances, array storage contains references: copying or separating the array does not clone the objects, so mutating an element's properties can be visible through both arrays. Copy-on-write also does not make concurrent mutation of the same variable safe. Separate tests for value semantics, object ownership, transient copying cost, and retained memory population.
followUps: How would you keep both values observable in an optimized experiment?
When is copying a small slice worth the immediate work?
pitfalls: Expecting assignment to eagerly copy buffers and every object.
Treating copy-on-write as safe concurrent mutation of one variable.

questions.prompt: Why can an 80-point thumbnail grid have a large memory peak? Separate compressed bytes, decoded pixels, cache retention, and simultaneous decoding.
questions.scenario: Several 4000-by-3000 JPEGs decode together on a scale-three display. The final cache is small. The report assumes small UIImageView bounds guarantee small decoded buffers.
questions.androidBridge: Android Bitmap decoding and thumbnail sampling offer a pixel-budget analogy. UIImageView bounds do not set ImageIO decode dimensions, and Objective-C autorelease lifetime differs from Kotlin garbage collection or coroutine suspension.
rubric: Calculates 48 million bytes for the four-byte pixel estimate.
Converts 80 points at scale three to roughly 240 pixels.
Downsamples before unnecessary full-source decoding.
Bounds simultaneous decodes and separately handles panoramas or multiple frames.
Separates estimated pixels, transient peak, retained objects, and measured footprint.
questions.answerHTML:
With the stated four-byte pixel estimate, 4000 × 3000 × 4 is 48 million bytes, about 45.8 MiB, before overhead. JPEG compression does not tell you decoded size. At scale three, 80 points suggests about 240 pixels per side. A small view or scaling an already decoded image does not ensure decoding used that smaller size. These calculations are estimates, not measured process memory.

Use a bounded ImageIO thumbnail path with orientation transformation, then verify output dimensions and quality. A longest-edge bound preserves aspect ratio; a panorama filling a square needs a separate crop or accepted-quality policy. Bound active decodes as well as retained cache cost, because several large intermediates can dominate the peak. Inspect allocations, footprint, and route-exit retention independently. An autorelease pool releases some temporary Objective-C objects when its synchronous scope ends. It should not enclose await or drain future callbacks. Compare equivalent source fixtures and appearance, and label pixel arithmetic as estimated until actual memory evidence exists.
followUps: What evidence separates a decode peak from a retained screen cycle?
What extra limits apply to animated or untrusted images?
pitfalls: Budgeting decoded cache from compressed file bytes.
Expecting small view bounds to guarantee downsampling.

questions.prompt: Outline a positive-window task-group loader that returns input order. Explain what it bounds and how it preserves cancellation and failure.
questions.scenario: The batch creates one task per input, then waits for permits. After cancellation it compactMaps missing outputs and returns a shorter success.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine workers or a semaphore suggest bounded execution. Swift task groups return completion order and join their children; a semaphore around thousands of created tasks, in either language, does not bound queued captures or payload bytes.
rubric: Starts at most the positive limit and replaces work after completion.
Returns indices and keeps output mutation in the parent.
Checks cancellation before new admission and publication.
Preserves errors and cancellation instead of incomplete success.
Separates active tasks, queued work, payload bytes, and request rate.
questions.answerHTML:
Reject a nonpositive window and return empty for empty input. Start at most the allowed number of children. Each returns its input index and immutable value. The parent puts completed values into their slots and, after checking cancellation, starts at most one replacement. Only the parent mutates output. Completion order may differ from input order, but indices keep the returned array correct.

Let meaningful child failure escape under the declared policy so the structured scope cancels and joins remaining work. Children must cooperate; the group cannot force an unresponsive legacy call to stop. Check cancellation before admission and before publishing. Validate that every expected output exists rather than using compactMap to disguise missing work as success. This window bounds initially created and active children, but not final output size, each payload's bytes, or requests per second. Give those separate budgets. Use gated fakes to complete later inputs first and verify ordering, peak active calls, empty input, and cancellation without timing sleeps.
followUps: What happens if a canceled fake never resumes?
How would you explicitly represent partial failure if it were allowed?
pitfalls: Calling thousands of permit-waiting tasks bounded memory.
Using compactMap to turn cancellation into shorter success.

questions.prompt: Own a shared loader under memory and energy limits. Compare coalescing and independent work, define loss policies, and plan evidence, rollout, and recovery.
questions.scenario: Visible and prefetched rows share downloads. Callback values arrive faster than decoding. Logout happens during transfer, and one departing waiter cancels work needed by everyone.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Flow suspension and shared coroutine ownership suggest demand and waiter policies. AsyncStream bufferingNewest drops buffered elements rather than suspending producers, and awaiting an unstructured Swift Task does not automatically propagate waiter cancellation.
rubric: Names shared-operation, waiter, cache-commit, and UI-publication owners.
Compares replaceable progress with required ordered-event delivery.
Separately budgets queued bytes, active work, priority, and rate.
Checks account epoch at cache commit and query generation before display.
Defines device evidence, staged adoption, and bounded fallback.
questions.answerHTML:
Coalescing means several consumers share one underlying operation. The service owns that operation; each consumer owns its interest. Define what cancellation means when one leaves and when the last leaves. Compare shared and independent requests with transfer, latency, and memory evidence. Give visible demand priority over optional prefetch through an explicit admission rule. A consumer losing interest is not automatically permission to cancel everyone else's work.

For streams, replaceable progress may use a newest-value buffer. Ordered tokens or commands need demand-aware delivery, a pull source, or explicit overflow failure and recovery. An element count is not a byte budget. Independently bound queued bytes, active transfers, decoding, and request rate. The cache owner checks account epoch, an ownership-period counter, where it commits. The UI owner checks query generation before display. Stage one consumer after gated cancellation/logout fixtures and matched device comparisons of throughput, p95, peak memory, and supported energy observations. Under pressure, stop optional admission and recover gradually; avoid restart storms. Keep a known-good loading policy for rollback and never report battery savings from request-count reduction alone.
followUps: What signals show useful coalescing versus visible work waiting behind prefetch?
How should a lossless stream recover after exceeding its byte budget?
pitfalls: Calling a dropping AsyncStream buffer producer backpressure.
Checking account only before a later unguarded cache write.

questions.prompt: Sketch stable deduplication with a membership set. Explain exact output, equality, expected work, and memory before claiming it is faster.
questions.scenario: Input is [b, a, b, c]. The baseline repeatedly scans its output. A proposed replacement converts directly to Set and returns its elements.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin LinkedHashSet suggests preserving first occurrence, but a plain Swift Set does not preserve the input-order contract. Swift String equality and hashing are not Java UTF-16 or byte-comparison semantics, so keep the declared identity policy.
rubric: Traverses input and appends newly inserted keys.
Predicts the complete ordered output [b, a, c].
Compares quadratic scans with expected linear membership work.
Accounts for hashing, projected keys, Unicode equality, and memory.
Checks semantics before comparable optimized measurements.
questions.answerHTML:
Walk the original input and keep a set of seen keys. Append only when seen.insert(key).inserted is true. For [b, a, b, c], output is [b, a, c]. The set answers whether the key occurred before; the output array preserves first-occurrence order. Returning the set's elements would change that promise because Set does not provide input order.

Repeated contains checks on a growing array have quadratic worst-case membership comparisons for many distinct items. Indexed membership usually reduces that work to expected linear behavior over the input, with additional storage. Hashing and equality still cost time, particularly for long strings, and projecting an identity key, extracting it from an item, can also cost time. Do not change case folding or normalization while claiming equivalence. Check complete outputs for empty, all-equal, all-distinct, mixed, and Unicode fixtures. Keep results observable under the same optimized configuration and construct fixtures outside a clearly named mapping-only interval. A microbenchmark can establish the mapping tradeoff; it does not independently establish screen responsiveness or energy gains.
followUps: How does projecting a key affect duplicate selection and cost?
Why might excessive reserved capacity worsen the memory tradeoff?
pitfalls: Returning unordered Set elements as stable output.
Calling expected complexity a measured device improvement.

questions.prompt: How would you separately test build speed and scrolling speed? Repair the mismatched build states and mapping intervals before attributing gains to module splitting.
questions.scenario: A no-op build is compared with a clean build on another toolchain. Set-backed mapping excludes fixture creation, while the baseline includes it. The report credits a module split for both compilation and scrolling.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle incremental-build and Kotlin algorithm analysis suggest separate investigations. Swift tools version, language mode, optimization, and generated module graph are independent inputs; faster type checking does not imply faster iOS execution.
rubric: Separates build-time and runtime hypotheses.
Matches clean, no-op, and edit-triggered preparation.
Inspects the build dependency chain and first useful bottleneck.
Uses equivalent runtime intervals and checks complete results.
States module overhead and pending screen-level evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
Compilation and runtime are different experiments. Compare clean with clean, no-op with no-op, and equivalent edits with each other. Keep host, compiler, destination, dependency graph, generated inputs, configuration, and cache rules fixed. Inspect the build timeline for the phase that holds up completion: type checking, dependency output, linking, resources, or scripts. Splitting modules can reduce rebuild scope but also adds graph overhead.

For runtime mapping, first verify complete output equivalence, ordering, duplicate policy, and errors. Construct fixtures outside both mapping-only intervals or include them consistently in a broader named operation. Use the same optimized configuration, keep results observable, alternate matched runs, and retain raw samples. Expected algorithm growth predicts a candidate but is not measured speed. A faster build or mapping does not establish scrolling improvement. That needs a separate stable-identity gesture experiment and hitch evidence. Correct the report's mismatched denominators before attributing either result to the module change.
followUps: Why can public and private edits have different incremental costs?
What evidence supports simplifying a typed expression before splitting a module?
pitfalls: Comparing clean and warm builds as equivalent work.
Including fixture creation in only one mapping measurement.

questions.prompt: Plan a controlled test of computing row projection on data changes instead of every body evaluation. What must be correct before you time it?
questions.scenario: The candidate computes the same projection when accepting a new data revision. Only a short profiler run exists. An async timeout was counted as completed latency.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android benchmark and macrobenchmark harnesses suggest distinct boundaries. An XCTest timing harness, signposted iOS interaction, and physical-device trace each prove different contracts; a timeout is not completed latency in either ecosystem.
rubric: Fixes revisions, fixture, and a hypothesis evidence could reject.
Checks order, identity, empty/errors, and cancellation before timing.
Separates diagnostic traces from matched confirmation samples.
Keeps outcomes and paired phases for each operation.
Labels measured, source-derived, theoretical, and pending claims.
questions.answerHTML:
Freeze baseline and candidate revisions, fixture, cache preparation, device group, and a testable hypothesis: avoiding unchanged projection should reduce repeated synchronous work. First check full equality, order, empty and error states, insertion identity, actions, and cancellation. A faster candidate that hides an action change or shows an old result is incorrect. Treat a timeout as unfinished work rather than successful latency.

Use a diagnostic trace to correlate projection work with relevant commit or hitch intervals. Then collect matched, lighter-instrumentation operation samples under a declared warm-up and outcome policy, alternating or randomizing batches to reduce drift. Record raw order, units, sample count, estimator, cache and thermal conditions, failures, cancellation, and invalid preparation. An async timeout is an unfinished operation, not a successful latency sample. Keep paired phase data rather than adding unrelated phase p95 values. Add memory route cycles only when the change affects retention or peak. The handoff separates arithmetic and source reasoning from executed tests and device measurements, with reproducible commands and artifacts. Hardware-dependent results remain pending until actually collected.
followUps: What profiler effects make lighter confirmation runs necessary?
What preparation details let another engineer reproduce the device group?
pitfalls: Timing before checking equivalent behavior.
Counting an unfinished timeout as completed latency.

questions.prompt: Own adoption of performance regression gates. Compare absolute user budgets with paired controls, define noise and rerun rules, and state failure and recovery decisions.
questions.scenario: The gate uses an arbitrary p95 threshold and retries until green. Simulator numbers are presented as phone smoothness and energy acceptance.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android performance CI suggests artifact retention and cohort budgets. Simulator XCTest baselines do not reproduce phone thermal, GPU, or energy behavior, just as host or emulator benchmarks cannot certify every Android device cohort.
rubric: Makes correctness the first mandatory gate.
Names fixture, budget, runner, and release-decision owners.
Compares absolute budgets with matched relative controls.
Uses observed variation and bounded rerun rules.
Stages enforcement and defines inspection, revert, or corrective-release outcomes.
questions.answerHTML:
Correctness is the first hard gate: old or incomplete output cannot pass. Name fixture, runner, budget, and release-decision owners. Derive thresholds for each device group from baseline observations, variation, and product needs. An absolute budget expresses an acceptable user wait. A paired control exposes changes in runner conditions. Compare both instead of picking a threshold merely to accept today's candidate.

Keep simulator CI and device release evidence separate. A simulator pass cannot certify phone rendering, memory pressure, or energy. Retain raw results, matching traces, failures, skips, and environmental changes so reviewers can distinguish regression from harness failure. Use a predeclared bounded rerun policy; repeated attempts until green hide instability. Stage new gates in observation mode, review noise and actionability, then enforce the validated boundaries. On failure, inspect or reproduce under the same protocol, revert the bounded candidate when regression is established, and use a corrective release if already distributed. Budget changes require an explained owner decision, not automatic relaxation.
followUps: What artifact distinguishes bad fixture preparation from a real regression?
When does a toolchain or fixture change require a new baseline?
pitfalls: Retrying until a passing result appears.
Treating simulator checks as phone energy acceptance.

questions.prompt: What do target, scheme action, configuration, destination, and service environment each choose? Why doesn't a scheme named Sandbox prove app identity or endpoint?
questions.scenario: The workspace can Run a Debug production app or Archive a Release sandbox app. Developers call either choice one flavor.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle product flavors and build types declared in Kotlin DSL form a variant graph, but an Xcode scheme is an action selection rather than one flavor. Swift compilation conditions, bundle identity, resources, and runtime endpoint are separate choices.
rubric: Defines each build choice and its job.
Separates optimization configuration from backend environment.
Explains that each scheme action can select different targets and settings.
Distinguishes declared settings, effective values, and built-artifact evidence.
Checks bundle identity and capabilities instead of trusting names.
questions.answerHTML:
A target defines one component and its output. A scheme chooses participants and settings separately for Run, Test, Archive, and other actions. A configuration supplies build settings; a destination selects platform and runtime. Service environment chooses which backend the app uses. These choices can combine differently: Debug can use production services and Release can use sandbox services when explicitly configured.

Scheme names describe intent, not the effective compiler conditions, installed bundle identifier, or endpoint. Follow the chosen action to its consuming target and configuration, then trace configuration includes, target overrides, resources, and the application's environment mapping. A user-defined build setting is not automatically readable by Swift code. Inspect bounded effective settings and compiler inputs, and verify the built bundle's identity and capabilities when artifact evidence is needed. Keep declaration, effective value, and observed behavior separate. Do not assume Xcode generates the same flavor cross-product as Gradle or that a directory named Sandbox participates in the selected action.
followUps: Why can Run and Archive in one scheme use different configurations?
How would you deliberately pass an environment build setting into app code?
pitfalls: Treating the scheme name as both a Gradle flavor and an endpoint.
Assuming Release always uses production services.

questions.prompt: Why does sandbox overwrite production and ignore the new Swift condition? Trace settings precedence and verify the compiler inputs and built app identity.
questions.scenario: An xcconfig appends COURSE_SANDBOX using inheritance. The target defines its own condition list. Both installed apps unexpectedly have the same bundle identifier.
questions.androidBridge: Android applicationIdSuffix and Kotlin/Java BuildConfig access suggest separate installation and behavior inputs. Xcode bundle identifiers and SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS follow layered setting precedence; they are not automatically generated from Gradle flavor semantics.
rubric: Identifies the selected action, target, configuration, and SDK.
Traces includes, inheritance, conditions, and target overrides.
Checks effective Swift conditions and compiler invocation.
Checks built bundle identity and matching capabilities.
Separates flag-selected behavior from endpoint configuration.
questions.answerHTML:
Identify the exact scheme action, target, configuration, and SDK for each build. Then follow included xcconfig files and later assignments. Settings precedence means one layer can override another. Inherited expansion preserves earlier list values only where used; a higher-priority target assignment can replace the list. Inspect effective Swift conditions and the compile command to establish whether COURSE_SANDBOX actually reaches this source.

For installation overwrite, inspect the built bundle identifier rather than the scheme label. Trace its prefix expansion and target overrides, then review compatible signing and capability inputs without dumping sensitive settings. The identifier governs installation identity; changing a Swift condition alone does not create another app identity. Separately inspect how the runtime endpoint is selected, because compiler flags do not automatically configure a server. Compare bounded declared, effective, and artifact observations, and classify any Release-only import failure by target dependency and conditional membership. Avoid a broad cache reset until the graph and precedence evidence identify an actual stale artifact.
followUps: Could inheritance keep an unwanted condition too?
What if the dependency exists in the generated graph but not the retained project?
pitfalls: Expecting an xcconfig append to survive every target override.
Changing only a Swift condition to create a separate installed app.

questions.prompt: Trace package, product, module, allowed requirement, and selected revision. Explain why a version-looking branch or framework suffix does not settle compatibility.
questions.scenario: The dependency audit includes a branch named 4.1.3. A mocks product has different linkage declarations in different active build routes.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle coordinates and dependency locks for Kotlin/Java modules suggest requirements versus selections. SwiftPM products expose target modules, and package resolution belongs to a consumer graph; Maven-style versions and AAR filenames do not define Swift linkage or module stability.
rubric: Separates package identity, exposed product, and imported module.
Distinguishes allowed requirement from selected revision.
Treats a version-looking branch as a branch.
Separates static/dynamic linking from framework packaging.
Distinguishes source, ABI, module, and runtime compatibility.
questions.answerHTML:
A package groups dependencies and build declarations. A product exposes targets to consumers; a target commonly defines an importable module. A requirement states what selections are allowed. The consumer's Package.resolved records what was chosen. A branch named 4.1.3 is still a branch, not an exact semantic release. A dependency's own lockfile does not force every downstream consumer to use its selection.

Static and dynamic describe linking behavior, not just whether an artifact ends in framework. Different graph routes can declare different linkage, which deserves consumer review rather than an automatic bug claim. Source compatibility asks whether code compiles against the API. ABI, the Application Binary Interface, defines compiled calls and layouts. Module stability supports consuming interfaces across compiler versions. Swift runtime ABI stability does not make arbitrary vendor binaries interchangeable. Check interfaces, platform variants, minimum OS, resources, and the consuming route. A resolved pin is neither proof of runtime execution nor a claim that the dependency is the latest available release.
followUps: Why are arm64 device and arm64 simulator different variants?
Which inputs would reproduce the consumer graph after a bounded change?
pitfalls: Reading a version-looking branch as an exact release pin.
Inferring linkage or compatibility from a framework filename.

questions.prompt: Plan review and adoption of VendorCodec. Compare source and binary options, assign owners, and define compatibility gates, rollout, and reconstructable recovery.
questions.scenario: The vendor offers an XCFramework with only a device build and a compiler-specific swiftmodule. It imports on one machine. The team wants immediate broad adoption.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java libraries packaged in Android AARs and native-library review suggest provenance and ABI coverage. XCFramework platform variants, swiftinterface module stability, and library evolution are separate Swift distribution contracts rather than JVM bytecode compatibility.
rubric: Names API, graph, packaging, provenance, and license reviewers.
Compares app-built source with independently distributed binaries.
Checks platform variants, interfaces, dependencies, resources, and runtime minimum.
Separates compile, link, load, and runtime availability evidence.
Stages one consumer and preserves prior artifact inputs for recovery.
questions.answerHTML:
An XCFramework packages platform variants of a binary library. One successful import is only one check. Assign API semantics, dependency graph, platform packaging, provenance, licensing, and data-behavior review. Compare rebuilding source with distributing the vendor binary. Inspect separate device and simulator variants, minimum OS, dependencies, resources, checksums, and interfaces. Equal CPU architecture does not make different platform variants interchangeable.

A compiler-specific swiftmodule can limit consumption across compiler versions; textual interfaces and appropriate distribution support address a different boundary from stable runtime ABI. Classify import, duplicate-symbol, missing-framework, and unavailable-API failures separately. Verify supported consumers through compile, link, artifact inspection, and runtime checks, including extensions when affected. Stage one bounded consumer after its semantic and integration evidence passes. Retain the prior manifest, resolution, generator/compiler inputs, resource contents, and binary checksum for reconstruction. Define containment and a corrective-build path if the candidate is distributed. Do not call checksum verification license approval, or assume rebuilding prior source downgrades installed clients.
followUps: When does BUILD_LIBRARY_FOR_DISTRIBUTION help, and why isn't it a universal setting?
What further evidence is needed when imports succeed but resources are missing?
pitfalls: Calling one import complete distribution compatibility.
Treating device and simulator slices as interchangeable because both are arm64.

questions.prompt: What evidence shows a library's actual job and migration status? Explain why ZDRxCore's name is misleading and what a promise-to-async wrapper preserves or changes.
questions.scenario: A guide calls the module RxSwift-based. The lesson finds a ReactiveKit dependency and re-export. PromiseKit bridges remain alongside guidance that prefers Swift Concurrency.
questions.androidBridge: Android dependencyInsight and RxJava-to-coroutines migrations suggest graph and consumer audits. A Swift module name does not establish its implementation, and converting a promise to async does not automatically inherit Kotlin structured cancellation semantics.
rubric: Uses active manifests, consumer dependencies, pins, and imports together.
Separates remote, local, system, vendored, and build-tool dependencies.
Uses ReactiveKit source evidence despite the misleading module name.
Distinguishes preferred direction from completed migration.
Checks bridge errors, buffering, cancellation, and completion ownership.
questions.answerHTML:
Follow the build route: manifest, consumer dependency, resolved revision, source membership, and imports. A name alone cannot show which library runs or why it is present. A pin may belong to tests or arrive through another dependency. A build plugin need not ship as a runtime SDK. Map responsibilities such as transport, models, UI, identity, and diagnostics to verified consumers.

The lesson's audit traces ZDRxCore to ReactiveKit despite RxSwift wording in a guide. That concrete dependency and re-export evidence should govern the explanation. The same audit finds PromiseKit bridges alongside guidance preferring Swift Concurrency; preference does not prove removal. An async wrapper changes the calling surface but does not automatically cancel underlying promise work or make its lifetime structured. Inspect task handles, continuation completion, actor isolation, and failure translation. Likewise, a publisher-to-stream bridge that finishes on failure can erase a thrown error distinction. State a migration claim per verified consumer and preserve empty success, failure, cancellation, and buffering semantics. Names and documentation alone cannot establish runtime adoption.
followUps: What evidence separates a declared SDK dependency from feature initialization?
How would you test a bridge that turns publisher failure into normal completion?
pitfalls: Teaching a library inferred only from a module name.
Claiming old code was removed because guidance prefers async.

questions.prompt: Design one catalog operation independent of vendor types. Assign interface, adapter, graph, and composition owners, and plan evidence, adoption, and recovery.
questions.scenario: The feature exposes vendor promises and resolves services while running. A wrapper renames many SDK methods but still treats offline failure like successful empty data.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin interface plus Dagger binding suggests separating product contract from adapter wiring. A runtime Swift container can fail during resolution rather than receiving Dagger's generated graph validation, and Swift async throws has separate cancellation rules.
rubric: Defines a narrow product operation with meaningful results and errors.
Names interface, adapter, graph, and composition-root owners.
Compares a stable seam with direct exposure and a broad wrapper.
